Today they see the first big danger of the quest play out, the Fury attack on the bus, and watch Percy's choices turn the prophecy's warnings into action.","enduringUnderstanding":"Heroes in myths are revealed by what they choose to do when they are afraid, and stories often test values like loyalty and bravery through a series of escalating challenges.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 18 students study Chapter 11 and practice clear pronoun reference and attribution when comparing texts. The homework excerpt from \"The Quest of Medusa's Head\" prepares students to compare a classic myth with Riordan's modern retelling.","performanceTask":"Today's analysis of how the bus fight raises the stakes of the quest builds the Performance Task skill of explaining how a challenge raises the stakes in a quest. The book-versus-film comparison also supports the adaptation analysis that Shared Stories, Shared Lessons requires."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"aura","definition":"a feeling or quality that seems to surround a person or thing","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"delicacy","definition":"a special, fine food; also, gentleness or care in handling something","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"withered","definition":"dried up, shrunken and weak, like a plant without water","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"dispelled","definition":"made something, such as a doubt or a feeling, go away","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"eerily","definition":"in a strange, creepy and frightening way","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"hideous","definition":"extremely ugly or horrible to look at","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"impulsive","definition":"acting quickly on a feeling without thinking first","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"careened","definition":"moved quickly and out of control, swerving from side to side","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"stampede","definition":"a sudden wild rush of a group, often in panic","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"submit","definition":"to give in to a stronger force or person","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the attitude a writer or narrator shows toward a subject, shown through word choice","tier":"support"},{"word":"stakes","definition":"what a character could win or lose in a situation","tier":"support"},{"word":"quest","definition":"a long, difficult journey taken to achieve an important goal","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 10, pp. 158–167"},{"title":"The Lightning Thief (2010 film), bus fight scene","author":"Directed by Chris Columbus","pages":"Film clip of the bus fight"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they know about heroes under pressure and connect the Oracle's warnings in Chapter 9 to the danger Percy faces in Chapter 10.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Heroes Under Pressure","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.3"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner: Think of a hero from a myth, movie or book. What is one choice that hero made when things got dangerous? What did that choice show about the hero?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does a character's choice in a dangerous moment tell us that a description of that character cannot?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When someone is in danger, you see what they really care about. A narrator can say someone is brave, but if the character runs toward the problem to save a friend, that shows it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we read the bus fight in Chapter 10. Watch for what Percy does when he is scared and what that shows about the hero he is becoming. Later we will compare how the book and the 2010 film show the same moment."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Listen for students who link bravery to loyalty, since both values appear in today's essential question."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students determine the meanings of key words from pp. 158–167 using context clues, word relationships and connotation, and practice fluent reading of the scene.","activities":[{"id":"lab-vocab-in-context","title":"Vocabulary in Context: Danger Words","minutes":7,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.5","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words in Context","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 10","pages":"pp. 158–167"},{"type":"directions","text":"Find each word in the chapter. Reread the sentence and the sentences around it. Underline clues, then write your own meaning in your Personal Dictionary. Words: aura (p. 159), delicacy (p. 160), withered (p. 161), dispelled (p. 161), eerily (p. 162), hideous (p. 164), impulsive (p. 164), careened (p. 164), stampede (p. 165), submit (p. 166)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's model with *careened*. Read the sentence on p. 164 and notice the surrounding action. If the bus is out of control and swerving, *careened* must mean moving fast and wildly. Compare it with *drove*. Both mean the bus moved, but *careened* adds danger and panic. That difference is a nuance, and it shapes the tone."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How are *hideous* and *eerily* different in the feeling they create, even though both are scary words?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Hideous is about how awful something looks, so it's a strong, disgusted feeling. Eerily is about a creepy, strange way something happens, so it makes me feel nervous and uneasy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Delicacy* has more than one meaning. Which meaning fits on p. 160, and what clues helped you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 160 it fits the meaning of a special food because the surrounding sentences talk about food being offered. The other meaning, gentleness, doesn't make sense there."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Check each word against the exact page and sentence before teaching, since editions can differ slightly. Cover *aura*, *withered* and *dispelled* by having partners share the clues they underlined. Spend the most time on multiple-meaning *delicacy* and the connotation difference between *hideous* and *eerily*."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["L.6.4"],"stem":"In a sentence describing a bus that *careened* down the road, which meaning of *careened* best fits?","choices":[{"text":"moved slowly and carefully","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses the meaning. The scene is a chaotic fight, so the bus is not moving carefully."},{"text":"moved fast and out of control, swerving","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The danger and chaos in the surrounding sentences show the bus was swerving wildly."},{"text":"stopped suddenly","correct":false,"rationale":"A sudden stop is a different action. Nothing in the clues suggests the bus stopped."},{"text":"turned into a different vehicle","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the word with a change of form. The context describes how the bus moved."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in using context clues and word relationships to determine the meanings of vivid action and description words.","sayAsk":"Have students say each word aloud with a partner and act out careened and stampede. Ask: What clue in the sentence helped you? Offer frames: I think ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. ___ and ___ both mean ___, but ___ feels more ___. Allow students to connect words to cognates, such as horrible/hideous or impulsivo/impulsive.","watchFor":"If students guess a meaning without checking the sentence, then prompt: What words around it support your guess? If students treat careened and drove as the same, then ask: Which one shows more danger? Success looks like students citing a specific clue and explaining a nuance between two words."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Using context to find a word's meaning","tryThis":"Give a three-step card: 1) Read the sentence. 2) Underline two clue words. 3) Say, This word means ___ because ___. Pair with a partner to act out the action words."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students write two sentences using *impulsive* and *submit* about different characters, then explain how each word's connotation reveals the character's attitude."}]}]},{"id":"lab-fluency-read-aloud","title":"Fluency: Read the Tension","minutes":3,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Partner Reading","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, take turns reading a paragraph aloud from the start of the bus fight (around p. 164). Read with the pace and expression the scene calls for. Slow down for creepy moments and speed up for fast action. Switch readers after each paragraph."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Model one sentence first. Read a creepy sentence slowly, then an action sentence quickly. Listen for pauses at punctuation and expression that matches the vocabulary words. Offer quick feedback: Your voice made *eerily* sound eerie."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students analyze how Percy's choices in the bus fight reveal his heroism and how the episode raises the stakes of the quest. Part B: Students compare the book scene with the 2010 film using a two-column organizer.","activities":[{"id":"lia-close-read-percy-choices","title":"Part A: Percy's Choices Under Pressure","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 10","pages":"pp. 158–167"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the bus fight on pp. 158–167. Annotate: 1) Put a star by each moment where Percy makes a choice. 2) Underline words that show how he feels. 3) Circle words the narrator uses that show tone. Then record two choices and the evidence in your notes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When we cite evidence, we quote or paraphrase exact details and then explain what they show. A choice is what a character does when other options exist. Percy's choices show his values, and the narrator's word choices, like *hideous* and *eerily*, show how dangerous and frightening the moment feels."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy do when the danger begins, and what is he thinking or feeling? Cite the text."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On pp. 164–165, Percy is scared of the hideous creature but he still acts to protect Grover and Mrs. Dodds' passengers instead of running away. The text shows his fear in the description, but his choices show he puts others first."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's choice to protect his friend reveal about the kind of hero he is becoming?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It reveals that loyalty matters to him. He isn't a perfect or fearless hero yet, since he's scared and sometimes impulsive, but he chooses to act for his friend, which is a value myths celebrate."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Is Percy brave because he isn't afraid, or for another reason? Use a detail to explain."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He's brave because he acts even though he's afraid. The narrator's words like *eerily* and *hideous* show how frightening it is, and he still makes a choice to face it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Verify the exact moments and quotations on pp. 158–167 in your edition before class and have a few ready to point to. Steer students toward quoting specific lines rather than summarizing the whole fight. If students say Percy has no fear, redirect to the narrator's description of his reactions."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"stem":"What do Percy's choices during the bus fight best reveal about him?","choices":[{"text":"He is already a fearless, perfect hero who is never scared.","correct":false,"rationale":"This ignores the text's descriptions of his fear. He is becoming a hero, not already a flawless one."},{"text":"He acts out of loyalty and bravery, protecting others even though he is afraid.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. His choices to protect his friend despite the danger show loyalty and courage, values myths celebrate."},{"text":"He wants to avoid trouble and hide until it is over.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is the opposite of what he does. He steps toward the danger instead of hiding."},{"type":"text","text":"","correct":false,"rationale":"placeholder"}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in citing evidence and describing how a character's choices reveal his values.","sayAsk":"Ask students to point to the line first, then explain. Offer frames: On page ___, Percy ___. This shows that he values ___. The narrator uses the word ___ to make the scene feel ___. Percy acts ___ (bravely / quickly / loyally) when ___. Invite students to add adverbials to sentences, such as: Percy fights bravely, in the aisle of the bus, because he wants to protect his friend.","watchFor":"If students retell the fight without explaining, then prompt: What does that choice show about Percy? If students give an opinion only, then ask: Which words in the text make you think that? Success looks like a cited detail, an explanation of the value it shows, and at least one adverbial adding how, where or why."}]},{"id":"lia-structure-raising-stakes","title":"Part A: How the Bus Fight Raises the Stakes","minutes":6,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.3","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A quest story is built from a series of challenges. Each challenge adds risk, so the stakes, what the hero could lose, grow as the story moves forward. The bus fight is one episode in that series. It follows the Oracle's prophecy in Chapter 9 and shows that the danger is now real."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think about the bus fight, then share with a partner: What is at risk in this episode? How does it make the quest more dangerous or more urgent than before? Record one sentence: This episode raises the stakes by ___, which moves the quest forward because ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this episode fit into the quest's overall structure?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It is an early challenge that shows enemies are actively attacking Percy and his friends. It raises the stakes because they could lose a friend or their lives, and it pushes the quest forward by forcing them to keep going toward the next challenge."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the bus fight connect to what the Oracle said in Chapter 9?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Oracle warned that the quest would be dangerous and that there would be betrayal and loss. The bus fight makes that danger real, so we start to believe the prophecy is coming true."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining how one scene fits into a larger plot structure using cause-and-effect language.","sayAsk":"Offer frames: This episode raises the stakes because ___. As a result, the quest becomes ___. This challenge comes after ___ and before ___. Have partners rehearse the frame aloud before writing.","watchFor":"If students only summarize the scene, then ask: What could the characters lose now that they could not before? If students are unsure of structure, then ask them to place the episode on a simple timeline of quest challenges. Success looks like a stakes statement with a cause-and-effect link to the next part of the quest."}]},{"id":"lia-book-vs-film","title":"Part B: Book vs. Film Organizer","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.7","RL.6.1","RL.6.6","L.6.5"],"routine":"Two-Column Graphic Organizer and Viewing","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 10 and the 2010 film bus fight scene","pages":"pp. 158–167 and film clip"},{"type":"directions","text":"Create a two-column organizer. Label the left column The Book and the right column The 2010 Film. In the left column, take notes on the bus fight from the text: the emotions the main characters feel and the tone the narrator uses, with specific words or details. Then watch the film version of the scene. In the right column, answer the same questions about the film. Below the organizer, write notes contrasting what you see and hear in your mind when you read with what you perceive when you watch and listen."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"As we did before, the goal is to compare how two versions tell the same event. In the book, words like *hideous* and *eerily* build the tone and Percy's thoughts are shared by the narrator. In a film, tone comes from sound, music, camera angles, lighting, actors' faces and special effects. Pay attention to what is the same, what changes and why a filmmaker might choose it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Make sure the film clip is cued before class. Show it once straight through, then replay a short portion if needed. Students should complete the left column before viewing. Remind students to focus on emotions and tone, not just plot differences."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What emotions do the characters feel in the book, and how does the narrator's tone shape them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the book, Percy feels scared and confused, but also determined to protect his friend. The narrator's tone is tense and creepy because of words like *eerily* and *hideous*, and we get Percy's thoughts, which make it feel personal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you see and hear in the film that you imagined differently while reading?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the film, the music and the loud sound effects made it feel more like an action scene than a creepy one. I could see the creature's face, but in my head while reading it was scarier because I imagined it myself."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why might the filmmakers have made a choice that is different from the book, and how does that change the way you see Percy as a hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Filmmakers may use fast action and sound to keep the audience excited. In the film, Percy's fear is shown by his face instead of his thoughts, so I notice his bravery less and his fighting more."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in closely reading and viewing, and in evaluating how language and visuals each create tone.","sayAsk":"Provide frames: In the book, the narrator describes ___ with the words ___, which creates a ___ tone. In the film, the ___ (music / lighting / actor's face) shows ___. When I read, I picture ___, but when I watch, I notice ___. One difference is ___; one similarity is ___. Encourage students to add adverbials such as quickly, in the dark or with a shaky voice.","watchFor":"If students only list plot differences, then prompt: How does the scene feel in each version? What creates that feeling? If students write vague notes like it was better, then ask for a specific word or image. Success looks like specific text details on the left, specific film details on the right, and a contrast between reading and viewing."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Noting tone and emotion in the book and the film","tryThis":"Give a word bank of feeling words (tense, creepy, terrified, determined, exciting) and ask students to pick one for each column, then find the detail that supports it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how one filmmaker choice changes how brave or loyal Percy seems, and to rewrite one sentence of the book so it matches the film's tone."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize what Percy's choices reveal and how the bus fight raises the quest's stakes.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Exit Reflection","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the paragraph: In the bus fight, Percy shows that he is becoming a hero who values ___. One detail that shows this is ___. This episode raises the stakes of the quest because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the bus fight, Percy shows that he is becoming a hero who values loyalty. One detail that shows this is that he acts to protect Grover even though he is scared. This episode raises the stakes of the quest because it proves the danger from the prophecy is real and that his friends could be hurt."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task you will explain how a challenge raises the stakes in a quest. Today's sentence is practice for that skill."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Students continue the story and connect it to a classic myth.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Reading and Annotation","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read the summary of Chapter 11 (pp. 168–top of 178, ending \"...into the garden of statues.\"). 2) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief Chapter 10 (p. 178, beginning \"Aunty Em directed us...\"–p. 187). 3) Read and annotate the excerpt from \"The Quest of Medusa's Head\" in Old Greek Stories. As you read, mark one detail that shows a character's choice and one detail that raises the stakes."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students analyze how Percy's choices during the Chapter 10 bus fight (pp. 158–167) reveal loyalty and bravery, and how the episode raises the stakes as one challenge in the quest.
